title: Hosted API minimal handshake and tool escape routes — PRD sketch
content:
Context and intent

This is a rough PRD sketch exploring a minimal handshake model for the hosted API streaming surface that prioritizes low-latency happy-paths while providing well-defined escape routes for tool failures, client disconnects, and degraded model fallbacks. Focus areas: streaming ergonomics, tool-calling semantics, compact structured output, and SDK-friendly developer primitives.

Why this problem now
- Multiple apps hit latency SLOs when we force full upfront capability negotiation for every session.
- Tool integrations increase tail latency and brittle failure modes.
- Teams want a single obvious SDK surface that works for low-latency clients (mobile, browser) and server apps.

Goals
- Define a minimal handshake that allows immediate token streaming while admitting later capability negotiation.
- Provide explicit, observable escape routes for tool call failures and model fallbacks (no opaque retries).
- Keep SDK surface small and predictable: 3 primitives max for streaming + tool calls.
- Ensure structured outputs remain parseable under partial stream and resume scenarios.

Non-goals
- Full formal spec for session persistence or cross-region mirroring (we'll link to session-resume PRD later).
- Guaranteeing every third-party tool is transactional; we provide safety modes and best-effort semantics.

Short proposal (high level)
1) Minimal handshake: client sends a tiny StartFrame with: client-id, session-hint, optional capability mask (can be empty). Server responds immediately with an AckFrame and then starts streaming tokens. Capability negotiation can happen asynchronously mid-stream via CapabilityUpdate frames.
   - StartFrame is intentionally minimal: 1 RTT before tokens (often piggybacked on TLS).
   - AckFrame carries a session token and a small list of accepted capability tags.

2) Tool call model: tool calls are declared inline as ToolFrames embedded in the token stream (sparse markers).
   - Tools have 3 possible policies per-call: guaranteed, best-effort, local-emulate.
   - If a guaranteed tool fails, server emits a FailureFrame and can optionally emit a CompensatingActionFrame (if defined by client).
   - Best-effort: server will attempt the call but will continue streaming with a ToolFallbackFrame after X seconds.
   - local-emulate: SDK can optionally emulate tool results on the client (safe for certain tool types).

3) Structured output tolerance: every structured object sent in the stream is bracketed with a Frame header and a compact checksum. Partial frames are allowed; clients must be able to resume parse on reconnect using frame indices.
   - Structured Output = JSON-ish but delivered in discrete frames with types: OBJECT_START, FIELD_CHUNK, OBJECT_END, META.
   - We include a small schema-hash in OBJECT_START so clients can detect mismatches quickly and downgrade to text if needed.

4) SDK ergonomics (developer primitives): aim for 3 primitives across languages: startStream(), onFrame(callback), sendEvent()/continue().
   - startStream() returns a StreamHandle that emits frame events.
   - onFrame() receives typed frames (token, toolRequest, toolResponse, failure, meta) but SDK should expose higher-level helpers: waitForTool(), resumeAfterFailure().
   - Default SDK behavior: non-blocking token stream; tool calls use a Promise-like API with configurable timeout policy.

Fallback / escape routes (concierge patterns)
- Connection hiccup: client reconnects with resumeToken (from AckFrame) + lastFrameIndex. Server resumes stream from nearest checkpoint and replays minimal meta to allow client to rehydrate local UI.
- Tool latency beyond threshold: server emits ToolFallbackFrame with: fallback_mode, latency_ms, reason_code. Fallback modes: omit, best-effort-synth, route-to-fallback-model, defer-to-client.
- Tool error with side-effects: server marks session as TAINTED and emits TaintedFrame with audit id and suggested compensating actions.
- Schema mismatch: OBJECT_START includes schema-hash. If mismatch, server sends SchemaFallbackFrame and either: 1) embed textual fallback, 2) stream a best-effort schema-rewrite, or 3) close with structured error depending on policy.

Telemetry and observability
- Minimum events to emit per session: handshake-time, ack-latency, first-token-time, tool-call-latency (per-policy), tool-fallback-rate, schema-mismatch-rate, partial-resume-success.
- Add field-level counters for structured output parse errors.
- Expose per-route SLOs in Console: token P50/P95/P99, tool-fallbacks per 1000 calls, average schema rewrite time.

Compatibility matrix (backwards-safe)
- New minimal handshake must accept clients that include full capability lists (we ignore extras).
- Old clients that expect full upfront capability negotiation will continue to work via a compatibility flag: compatMode: full-negotiate in StartFrame.

Tradeoffs considered
- Minimal handshake saves ~1 RTT on average but complicates early tool routing (we defer some routing decisions until after stream start).
- Allowing client-side emulation reduces server load but increases risk of inconsistent results; should be opt-in and audited.

Implementation sketch (phases)
Phase 0 (alpha): server-side ack + token streaming on minimal StartFrame. SDKs: JS and Python shallow impls with onFrame and startStream. Telemetry hooks present. -> 6 weeks
Phase 1 (tool policies): add ToolFrame types, implement best-effort and fallback emission. Basic admin knobs for timeouts. -> 8 weeks
Phase 2 (structured output frames + schema-hash): implement OBJECT_START/END frames and partial-resume semantics; add Console charts. -> 6 weeks
Phase 3 (resume/taint/compensation): full production rollout with customer-facing docs and migration guide. -> 4 weeks + ramp

Open questions / TODOs
- Timeouts: what should default tool-call timeout be for guaranteed vs best-effort? (suggest 2s/6s)
- Audit model for client-side emulation: how to surface divergence?
- Schema-hash format: SHA1? truncated CRC32? tradeoffs for size vs collision safety.
- SDK helper ergonomics: blocking waitForTool() vs streaming-first Promises. Which maps better to mobile async patterns?
- Backpressure: how to surface server-side backpressure to small-footprint clients without breaking streaming semantics?

Immediate next actions
- Product: finalize default timeout recommendations and failure codes (Avery) — due 2026-03-17
- Eng infra: spike server ack + token streaming prototype (Diego) — 2w
- SDK: ship JS/TS minimal-wrappers prototype with startStream/onFrame (Priya) — 3w
- Security: review taint/audit framing for PII (Samira) — 1w

Notes and references
- Related tickets: JIRA-1248 (streaming resume spike), JIRA-1312 (tool policy experiment).
- Quick sketch diagram: see CONFLUENCE-HostAPI-MinimalHandshakes (linked).

Rough appendix (handshake frame shapes, human-readable)
- StartFrame: {client_id, session_hint?, capability_mask?}  // small, optional fields
- AckFrame: {session_token, accepted_capabilities[], schema_version, resume_index}
- TokenFrame: {frame_index, token_chunk}
- ToolFrame: {tool_id, call_id, policy, payload_ref}
- ToolFallbackFrame: {call_id, fallback_mode, latency_ms, reason}
- FailureFrame: {code, message, advice}

The above shapes are aspirational; we will produce a formal wire-spec once we settle timeouts and schema-hash format.

---
Notes to self: keep this doc intentionally light on wire-level verbosity so we can iterate in sync with SDK prototypes. Avoid feature-creep: start small, measure, then add policy knobs.
